en: Thus have I heard— The Mahāsuññata Sutta (The Greater Discourse on Voidness), Majjhima Nikāya 122.
On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling among the Sakyans at Kapilavatthu in the Nigrodha Park.
Then, in the morning, the Blessed One dressed, took his bowl and robe, and entered Kapilavatthu for alms.
Having walked for alms in Kapilavatthu, after his meal, returning from his almsround, he went to the monastery of Kāḷakhemaka the Sakyan for his midday rest.
Now at that time, many lodgings had been prepared in the monastery of Kāḷakhemaka the Sakyan.
The Blessed One saw the many lodgings prepared in the monastery of Kāḷakhemaka the Sakyan,
and having seen them, this thought occurred to the Blessed One:
“Many lodgings have been prepared in the monastery of the Sakyan Kāḷakhemaka.
Are there many bhikkhus staying here?
Now at that time, the Venerable Ānanda was making robes in the monastery of the Sakyan Ghaṭā together with a number of bhikkhus.
Then, in the evening, the Blessed One emerged from seclusion and went to the dwelling of Ghaṭāya the Sakyan; having arrived, he sat down on the prepared seat.
Once seated, the Blessed One addressed the Venerable Ānanda:
“Ānanda, many lodgings have been prepared in the dwelling of Kāḷakhemaka the Sakyan.”
“Are there many bhikkhus dwelling here?
“There are many, Bhante; many seats have been prepared in the monastery of the Sakyan Kāḷakhemaka.
Many bhikkhus dwell here.”
“Venerable sir, the time for making robes has come for us.

“Ānanda, a bhikkhu does not shine who delights in company, who takes pleasure in company, who is devoted to delighting in company; who delights in a group, who takes pleasure in a group, who rejoices in a group.
Indeed, Ānanda, that bhikkhu who delights in company, who takes pleasure in company, who is devoted to delighting in company...”

"It is impossible, Ānanda, that a bhikkhu who delights in company and rejoices in company will obtain at will, without difficulty, and without hardship, that happiness which is the happiness of renunciation, the happiness of seclusion, the happiness of peace, and the happiness of enlightenment.
But for that bhikkhu, Ānanda, who dwells alone, withdrawn from company— "

"It is possible that he will obtain at will, without difficulty, and without hardship, that happiness which is the happiness of renunciation, the happiness of seclusion, the happiness of peace, and the happiness of enlightenment— it is for this that it is possible. Yet, Ānanda,
that bhikkhu who delights in company, takes pleasure in company, is devoted to delighting in company, and delights in the crowd..."

That a monk who delights in the group and rejoices in the group will dwell having attained either the temporary liberation of mind that is lovely, or the unshakeable liberation that is not temporary—this is impossible.

But for that monk, Ānanda, who dwells alone, withdrawn from the group, this is possible: that he will dwell having attained either the temporary liberation of mind that is lovely, or the unshakeable liberation that is not temporary.
"It is possible, Ānanda, that one might attain and dwell in a pleasant, temporary liberation of mind, or even an unshakable, non-temporary liberation of mind— this is a possibility. However, Ānanda,
I do not see even a single form such that, for one who is attached to and delights in that form, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair would not arise due to its change and alteration."
Moreover, Ānanda, this is the dwelling awakened to by the Tathāgata, namely:
to enter and dwell in internal emptiness through non-attention to all signs.
If, Ānanda, while the Tathāgata is dwelling in this dwelling, there should come to him monks, nuns, laymen, laywomen, kings, royal ministers, members of other sects, or followers of other sects.
In this regard, Ānanda, with a mind inclined toward seclusion, sloping toward seclusion, leaning toward seclusion, withdrawn,
delighting in renunciation, and entirely free from all things that are the basis for the taints, the Tathāgata speaks only such discourse as is connected with sending [others] forth.
Therefore, Ānanda, if a bhikkhu should wish:
‘May I dwell having entered upon internal emptiness,’ Ānanda, that bhikkhu should steady his mind right within, settle it, unify it, and concentrate it.
And how, Ānanda, does a bhikkhu steady his mind right within, settle it, unify it, and concentrate it?
Here, Ānanda, secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states, a bhikkhu enters and dwells in the first jhāna … [and so on] …
He enters and dwells in the second jhāna … the third jhāna … the fourth jhāna.
In this way, Ānanda, a bhikkhu steadies his mind internally, settles it, unifies it, and concentrates it.
He directs his attention to internal emptiness.
As he directs his attention to internal emptiness, his mind does not leap forward into emptiness, does not find confidence in it, does not become settled in it, and is not liberated by it.
This being so, Ānanda, a bhikkhu understands thus:
"When I attend to internal emptiness, my mind does not leap forward into internal emptiness, does not find confidence in it, does not become settled in it, and is not liberated by it.
In this way, he is clearly comprehending with regard to that matter.
Thus he attends to external emptiness …pe… he attends to internal-and-external emptiness …pe… he attends to imperturbability.
As he attends to imperturbability, his mind does not leap forward toward it, does not find confidence in it, does not settle down in it, and is not liberated in it.
Being thus, Ānanda, the bhikkhu understands:
“While I am attending to imperturbability, my mind does not leap forward toward it, does not find confidence in it, does not settle down in it, and is not liberated in it.”
Thus he is fully aware therein.
Therefore, Ānanda, that bhikkhu should steady his mind right within, settle it, unify it, and concentrate it upon that very same original sign of concentration.
He directs his attention to internal emptiness.
As he attends to emptiness internally, his mind leaps forward into internal emptiness, gains confidence, becomes settled, and is liberated.
Being thus, Ānanda, the bhikkhu understands:
“As I attend to emptiness internally, my mind leaps forward into internal emptiness, gains confidence, becomes settled, and is liberated.”
Thus he is fully aware therein.
He directs his attention to external emptiness … [as before] … he directs his attention to both internal and external emptiness … [as before] …
He directs his mind toward the imperturbable.
As he directs his mind toward the imperturbable, his consciousness leaps forward into it, gains confidence in it, becomes settled in it, and is liberated in it.
When this is the case, Ānanda, the bhikkhu understands it thus:
‘As I attend to the imperturbable, my mind leaps forward into the imperturbable, gains confidence in it, becomes settled in it, and is liberated in it.
Thus he is clearly comprehending in that regard.
Now, Ānanda, if while that bhikkhu is dwelling in this abiding his mind inclines toward walking, he walks back and forth.
‘While I am walking thus, no evil unwholesome states—such as covetousness or dejection—will flow into me.
In this way, he is clearly comprehending therein.
If, Ānanda, while that bhikkhu dwells in this dwelling, his mind inclines toward standing, he stands:
‘While I am established thus, evil unwholesome states such as covetousness and dejection will not flow over me.
Thus he is clearly comprehending in that regard.
If, Ānanda, while that bhikkhu dwells in this dwelling, his mind inclines toward sitting, he sits down:
‘While I am sitting thus, no evil unwholesome states—such as covetousness or dejection—will flow in upon me.
In this way, he is clearly comprehending in that regard.
If, Ānanda, while that bhikkhu dwells in this dwelling, his mind inclines toward lying down, he lies down:
‘While I am lying down in this way, covetousness, dejection, or other evil, unwholesome states will not flow into me.
Thus he is clearly comprehending in that regard.
If, Ānanda, while that bhikkhu is dwelling in this abiding, his mind inclines toward talk, he thinks:
‘Whatever talk is low, vulgar, worldly, ignoble, and unbeneficial—which does not lead to disenchantment, dispassion, cessation, peace, direct knowledge, enlightenment, or Nibbāna; that is to say:
talk of kings, talk of thieves, talk of ministers, talk of armies, talk of dangers, talk of battles, talk of food, talk of drinks, talk of clothing, ...’
Talk about beds, talk about garlands, talk about perfumes, talk about relatives, talk about vehicles, talk about villages, talk about towns, talk about cities, talk about districts,
talk about women, talk about liquor, talk about streets, talk about wells, talk about ancestors, talk about various matters, tales of the world, tales of the ocean,
or talk about how one comes to be and how one does not come to be— such as this.
"How shall I not speak?"—
thus one is fully aware in that regard.
And as for this talk, Ānanda, which is conducive to effacement, favorable to the removal of mental hindrances, and leading exclusively to disenchantment...
It leads to dispassion, cessation, peace, direct knowledge, enlightenment, and Nibbāna; that is to say:

talk on fewness of desires, talk on contentment, talk on seclusion, talk on non-association, talk on the arousal of energy, talk on virtuous behavior, talk on concentration, talk on wisdom, talk on liberation, and talk on the knowledge and vision of liberation: thinking, "I shall speak such talk."
Thus he is fully aware therein.
If, Ānanda, while that bhikkhu dwells in this dwelling, his mind inclines toward thoughts, he reflects:
"Those thoughts which are inferior, vulgar, worldly, ignoble, and unbeneficial, which do not lead to disenchantment, dispassion, [cessation, peace, direct knowledge, enlightenment, and Nibbāna]..."

‘Such thoughts as sensual thought, ill-will thought, and cruelty thought do not lead to cessation, nor to peace, nor to direct knowledge, nor to full awakening, nor to Nibbāna; thus, I shall not think such thoughts.
In this way, one is fully aware therein.

But as for those thoughts, Ānanda, which are noble, leading out, and lead the one who practices them toward the complete destruction of suffering—that is to say, thoughts of renunciation, thoughts of non-ill will, and thoughts of non-cruelty—one thinks: "I shall think such thoughts.
In this way, one is clearly comprehending therein.
There are, Ānanda, these five cords of sensual pleasure.
Which five?
Forms cognizable by the eye that are desirable, lovely, agreeable, pleasing, connected with sensual desire, and provocative of lust;
Sounds cognizable by the ear...
odors cognizable by the nose...
flavors cognizable by the tongue...
Tangible objects cognizable by the body that are desirable, lovely, agreeable, pleasing, connected with sensual pleasure, and provocative of lust— these, Ānanda,
are the five cords of sensual pleasure. In regard to these,
a bhikkhu should frequently examine his own mind:
‘Does there arise in me a mental preoccupation with one or another of these five strands of sensual pleasure?
If, Ānanda, upon reviewing, a bhikkhu understands thus:
‘There does arise in me a mental preoccupation with one or another of these five strands of sensual pleasure,’ [he should apply himself to its abandonment].”
This being so, Ānanda, a bhikkhu understands thus:
"That desire and lust for these five cords of sensual pleasure have not been abandoned by me.
In this way, he is clearly comprehending with regard to that.
But if, Ānanda, while reflecting, a bhikkhu understands thus:
‘In regard to these five cords of sensual pleasure, no mental preoccupation arises in me toward any one or another of them,’ then,
Ānanda, when this is the case, the bhikkhu understands it thus.
‘Whatever desire and lust there was for these five cords of sensual pleasure has been abandoned by me.
Thus he is clearly comprehending in that regard.
Ānanda, there are these five aggregates subject to clinging, wherein a bhikkhu should dwell contemplating their rise and fall:
‘Such is form, such is the arising of form, such is the passing away of form;
such is feeling...
such is perception...’
"Thus are volitional formations...
thus is consciousness, thus is the arising of consciousness, thus is the passing away of consciousness.
As he dwells contemplating the arising and passing away of these five aggregates of clinging, whatever conceit of "I am" there was regarding the five aggregates of clinging is abandoned.
This being so, Ānanda, a bhikkhu understands thus:
‘The conceit “I am” regarding these five aggregates of clinging has been abandoned by me.
In this way, he is clearly comprehending therein.
"These, Ānanda, are the states that are exclusively wholesome, leading to what is wholesome, noble, supramundane, and not entered upon by the Evil One.
What do you think, Ānanda,
seeing what benefit does a disciple deserve to follow the Teacher even when being sent away?"
“Venerable sir, our teachings are rooted in the Blessed One, guided by the Blessed One, and have the Blessed One as their refuge.
It would be well, venerable sir, if the Blessed One himself would explain the meaning of this statement; having heard it from the Blessed One, the bhikkhus will remember it.
“Ānanda, it is not fitting for a disciple to follow after the Teacher for the sake of such things as discourses, songs, and prose-expositions.”
For what reason?
Because for a long time, Ānanda, you have heard the teachings, retained them, mastered them through speech, examined them with the mind, and thoroughly penetrated them with right view.
And this discourse, Ānanda, which is conducive to effacement, favorable to the removal of mental hindrances, and leads exclusively to disenchantment...
It leads to dispassion, to cessation, to peace, to direct knowledge, to enlightenment, and to Nibbāna;

that is to say: talk on fewness of desires, talk on contentment, talk on seclusion, talk on non-association, talk on the arousal of energy, talk on virtue, talk on concentration, talk on wisdom, talk on liberation, and talk on the knowledge and vision of liberation—it is for the sake of such talk, Ānanda, [that one should speak].
"A disciple ought to follow the Teacher even if he is being sent away.
When this is so, Ānanda, there is a calamity for the teacher; when this is so, there is a calamity for the pupil; when this is so, there is a calamity for the practitioner of the holy life.
And how, Ānanda, is there a calamity for the teacher?"

In this case, Ānanda, a certain teacher resorts to a secluded lodging: a forest, the foot of a tree, a mountain, a glen, a hill-cave, a charnel ground, a jungle-thicket, or an open space, a heap of straw.
While he dwells thus withdrawn, brahmins and householders—both those from the towns and those from the countryside—come flocking to him.
As they flock to him, he seeks after their infatuation, falls into greed for them, and turns toward abundance.
"This, Ānanda, is called a teacher’s misfortune.

Through that teacher’s misfortune, evil unwholesome states—defiling, leading to renewed existence, accompanied by distress, resulting in suffering, and pertaining to future birth, aging, and death—were destroyed in him.
Such, Ānanda, is a teacher’s misfortune."
And how, Ānanda, does there come to be a calamity for a resident pupil?
It is when a disciple of that very teacher, while cultivating the seclusion of that teacher, resorts to a secluded lodging:
a forest, the foot of a tree, a mountain, a glen, a hill-cave, a charnel ground, a jungle-thicket, an open space, or a heap of straw.
As he dwells thus withdrawn, brahmins and householders—both those from the towns and those from the countryside—flock to him.
As these brahmins and householders, both from the towns and the countryside, flock to him, he develops infatuation for them, falls into greed, and turns toward abundance.
Ānanda, this is called a pupil who is a calamity.

"Because of the calamity concerning his pupil, evil, unwholesome states—defiling, leading to renewed existence, accompanied by distress, resulting in suffering, and pertaining to future birth, aging, and death—were destroyed in him.
In this way, Ānanda, there is a calamity concerning a pupil.
And how, Ānanda, is there a calamity concerning one who lives the holy life?"

"Here, Ānanda, a Tathāgata arises in the world, an arahant, perfectly enlightened, endowed with knowledge and conduct, well-gone, knower of the worlds, unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, teacher of gods and humans, the Buddha, the Blessed One.
He resorts to a secluded lodging: a forest, the foot of a tree, a mountain, a glen, a hillside cave, a charnel ground, a jungle thicket, an open space, or a heap of straw.
As he dwells thus withdrawn, brahmins and householders, both from towns and from the countryside, attend upon him."

Thus, while the brahmins, householders, town-dwellers, and country-folk were turning back [toward him], he did not seek after infatuation, he did not fall into greed, and he did not turn back toward abundance.
Furthermore, Ānanda, a disciple of that Teacher, cultivating the seclusion of that Teacher, resorts to a secluded lodging:
a forest, the foot of a tree, a mountain, a glen, a hill-cave, a charnel ground, a jungle-thicket, an open space, or a heap of straw.
As he dwells thus withdrawn, brahmins and householders—both those from the towns and those from the countryside—come to attend upon him.
As they attend upon him, he develops infatuation for those brahmins and householders, both from the towns and the countryside; he falls into greed and turns toward abundance.
This, Ānanda, is called a calamity for a practitioner of the holy life.

By means of the calamity that befalls the holy life, evil unwholesome states—corrupting, leading to renewed existence, accompanied by distress, resulting in suffering, and pertaining to future birth, aging, and death—are destroyed.
In this way, Ānanda, there is a calamity that befalls the holy life.

Now, Ānanda, compared to the calamity that befalls the teacher and the calamity that befalls the pupil, this calamity that befalls the holy life has a more painful result and a more bitter result; moreover, it leads to ruin.
Therefore, Ānanda, behave toward me as friends, not as enemies.
That will lead to your welfare and happiness for a long time.
And how, Ānanda, do disciples behave toward their teacher as enemies, not as friends?
In this case, Ānanda, the Teacher, out of compassion and seeking their welfare, teaches the Dhamma to his disciples, motivated by kindness:
“This is for your benefit; this is for your happiness.
Yet his disciples do not wish to hear, they do not lend an ear, they do not apply their minds to understand, and they proceed in defiance of the Teacher’s instruction.
In this way, Ānanda, disciples treat the Teacher as an enemy, not as a friend. And how, Ānanda, do disciples treat the Teacher as a friend, not as an enemy?

Here, Ānanda, the Teacher teaches the Dhamma to his disciples out of compassion, seeking their welfare, out of compassion: [he says: "This is for your benefit; this is for your happiness. Thus, Ānanda, disciples treat the Teacher as a friend, not as an enemy.
‘This is for your welfare; this is for your happiness.
His disciples listen, lend an ear, and apply their minds to understanding; they do not act contrary to the Teacher’s instruction.
In this way, Ānanda, disciples behave toward the Teacher as friends would, not as enemies.
Therefore, Ānanda, treat me with friendliness, not with enmity;
that will lead to your welfare and happiness for a long time.
Ānanda, I shall not exert myself for you in the same way as a potter exerts himself over unbaked clay.
"Having restrained it again and again, Ānanda, I shall speak;
having winnowed it again and again, Ānanda, I shall speak.
That which is the essence will remain."
Thus the Blessed One spoke.
The Venerable Ānanda, being uplifted, rejoiced in the words of the Blessed One.
The Mahāsuññata Sutta, the second, is finished.
